To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
the race of the patients, the age of the patients, and the sex of the patients all affect the diagnosis of psychiatric patients, while the status inconsistency of the patients has little effect.
status inconsistency is a relatively unimportant factor in the diagnosis of psychiatric patients.

1) status inconsistency does not explain the psychiatric diagnosis of the patients, 2) employment, occupation, and sex are moderately related to diagnosis, and 3) race is the single most powerful predictor of psychiatric diagnosis.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the process of social construction of psychiatric diagnosis.
the social construction of reality and the socialization of the psychiatrist in this process.
the relationship between the patient's status characteristics and the psychiatric dispositions of patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the psychiatric diagnosis of a patient is a function of the status inconsistency of the patient and of the social status of the patient as well as the social status and status inconsistency of the agent for diagnosis (psychiatric).

the psychiatric disposition of patients is a function of the status inconsistency, achieved status, ascribed status, employment, occupation age, and sex of the patient, and the race and age of the psychiatrists.
the social status of the patient, as well as the status inconsistency of the patient, is used in the diagnosis of the patient.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the social structure of the psychiatric hospital, the socialization of the psychiatrist, and the socialization of patients all affect the psychiatric disposition of a patient.
the diagnosis of psychiatric patients is a social construction, and that it is a function of the socialization of the psychiatrist and of the patient.
status inconsistency, although it may be related to psychiatric disorder, is not the primary determinant of psychiatric diagnosis.
The main takeaway from our work is that
status inconsistency, while it may be a powerful predictor in other social situations, is not a powerful predictor in psychiatric diagnosis.

the psychiatric diagnosis of a patient is not simply a function of the symptoms of the patient, nor is it simply a function of a psychiatrist's personal bias, but rather it is a function of the psychiatrist's socialization and the socialization of those who trained him or her.
status indicators are used in psychiatric diagnosis and that this is consistent with the general theory of social control.
